text: Okay, and we are recording again. We are out of executive session. The time is 945 a.m. During executive sessions, no decisions were made. No decisions were made. So what we would like to do at this point is take a vote on what was discussed in the executive session. Do we have any motions for approval? Motion to approve. So that was, who was that? Item five by Jim Grunberger, motion to approve item five. Okay, I'll second that. All in favor of item five? Aye. Aye. Aye. Any abstentions? So item five passes unanimously. Okay, and thank you, Tommy, yeah, thanks, Tom. If you wanted to drop off, you're more than welcome. I'm just giving a quick update on some of the things we're working on, and that'll be that. But I appreciate your time and your dedication to this program. No problem. Thank you, and thank you to all the members of the committee. We appreciate it. Thank you for your hard work. We appreciate it. Making the city safe. Thank you, Captain. Yeah, thank you, Captain. All right, so item five passes unanimously. On to item six. The last one is just a general public safety update on some of our camera and technological programs we have going on in the city. From out of my office, I'd just like to say that, you know, public safety technology remains one of our main priorities as an administration, especially when it comes to public safety. And I think as we go through these applications in this committee meeting, you could see why. Captain Scanlon referenced several investigations which led to positive outcomes and arrests being made based on camera technology. And in these times, it's just going to continue to evolve and grow. So with that said, it has been a big, very big priority of this administration and myself as a public safety director to continue to grow our public safety camera technologies. And it's very important that we continue to grow and keep up with times and make it a more valuable resource. But we need to do that methodically and not just be in a rush to expand for the sense of expand. My goal is to do this methodically with a long-term plan to make sure that we're maintaining equipment as we go along. There's a lot of servers and storage systems that have to be upgraded and replaced routinely. There's a lot of hardware and software upgrades that go into all these various technologies. And a quick example is some of these blue lights. These blue lights programs came into effect back in 2011. And prior to two years ago, there was basically no maintenance done on them at all. So we've been spending a lot of time and resources on making sure that if we are going to put forward these type of technological resources for our public safety and for our community, that we do it in a way that it's going to be a good investment and we're doing it in a way that we keep on top of it moving forward. So we're not just installing stuff, forgetting about it, and then in five years it's going to break down and, okay, the city moves on to the next project. We're trying to stay ahead of the curve when it comes to technology. So that's kind of the vision for what we're doing with technology enhancements for public safety. A lot of the focus has been on our public safety camera network and expanding that. You have heard from Steve Fritz, who's our main camera and traffic technician and supervisor. He's really been instrumental. They've been great partners with public safety in regards to using the infrastructure that we already have in place to monitor traffic, infrastructure, critical infrastructure, and sensitive locations throughout the city. Coming into this role, I think we were around 100 cameras city-wise. In the past three years, we've grown at a pretty steady pace. I think we're around 150 now. And within the next year, year and a half, we're looking to grow to have potentially over 200 cameras city-wise, specifically focusing on traffic, infrastructure, critical infrastructure, and sensitive locations. And the purpose of that is obviously to support large-scale gatherings. We do have a lot of gatherings in the city, and we want to make sure that we're keeping people safe and taking a proactive approach and utilizing our resources as effectively as possible. And that's what basically technology is doing. It's not taking care of problems for us. It's aiding us in being more effective in how we approach things from a public safety standpoint. The parks and coastline coverage, you heard from Kevin and Steve on that. And, again, as I stated, we had partnered with the PD on that as well and hit a lot of our parks and our coastline. The coastline has been a big factor and a big vulnerability, in my opinion. Our population growth is continuing to expand, and a lot of that growth is along the coastline. So we wanted to make sure that we had those capabilities where we have limited public safety resources in the event of emergencies. So we're making some pretty aggressive strides in that. And again, the goal is to enhance safety in recreational areas and out in some of those isolated areas on the water. Blue light camera, you heard from Steve. Again, currently we have 12 towers. And this program has been extremely successful. The inception of it was based on a very horrific incident that took place in early mornings at one of our parks in an isolated area. Hence, this program was started, and, you know, it's expanded quite a bit. Like I said, we're up to 12 towers, 24 cameras. Based on those approvals this morning, our goal is to add an additional nine blue lights towers throughout the city. And again, some of these parks are in highly dense areas, such as one of the new ones that's going up is in Kiwanis Park, which is right there in the heart of downtown Stanford. High traffic area, high foot traffic. And then another extreme of one of the ones that's almost ready to go operational is we just put one into Dorothy Heroid Park, which is a very isolated area, very poor cell service. So there's no cookie cutter mold for where we're putting cameras. I think by doing this approach of having a collaborative working group of people from operations, parks, public safety, assess, and community input, I'd like to say that because we have had a lot of requests for blue lights in specific areas. By having that collaborative approach in selecting locations and going through this process, I think we've done a very good job of identifying high traffic areas where the blue lights are going to be in a position to assist people, and also in those very isolated areas in some of our parks. So the blue light program continues to be very successful. The last thing I'd like to hit on is something that I'm very, very excited about as a public safety initiative. I know I had asked Kathy to email out to these committee members an information sheet that we had put together in regards to our expansion of our drone capabilities as a municipality. We're very excited to be launching our drone as a first responder program. We're targeting first week of October for it to be fully operational. Currently it is operational, but we're doing test runs and working out some of our protocol issues that we're trying to work out. But basically that program is a collaborative effort between our 911 center, our police department, and our fire department. And it consists of four drones. And we have had drones in the past, both fire and police. They've been operational, but those were more mobile drones deployed specifically on certain calls that would require drone footage or to assist in certain investigations. The DFR program is the first of its kind in Connecticut from a public safety standpoint. And basically how it's going to work is when a call comes in to dispatch, if it meets a certain criteria based on our policies and protocols, our dispatch supervisor at our 911 center will drop a pin on that location and the program is starting with two DFR drones. One is housed in the south side of the city and the other one is housed up north at a public safety facilities. And the drone will self-deploy out of a hangar and a docking station to that location. And this is going to be giving us coverage throughout our whole city within 90 seconds. From the time of that notification, from the time the supervisor clicks on that software deployment, we'll have live video footage over a scene and the drone will be hovering until either one of our pilots, our certified pilots from either the police department or fire department, depending on what the situation and incident is, have the capabilities of getting on and taking over piloting that drone to do whatever is necessary to support our first responders responding to that critical incident. But this is something, again, we're very excited about. It's really going to enhance our response protocols and to be able to get our eyes on something within 90 seconds in a critical incident is crucial. Fire is excited about it, PD is excited about it, and one last point I'd like to make on that is it's really a force multiplier, especially when we have, going back to the coastline coverage, between our plan to expand that coastline camera coverage and having those cameras facing outward so we can have some footage in those isolated areas out on the water. And now by having this drone capability through our DFR program to be able to respond out on the water is really going to be a game changer and it's going to be able to direct our, again, our first responders into a scene based on that footage that we're getting into the drones. So, if anybody has any questions, again, there was a lot of information that we put out on that informational sheet, but I'd love to have some conversation if anybody has any questions on that, and it's something that, again, we're really looking forward to, and I think it's going to take our public safety operation and our resources that we have available to our community to the next level. So, something that, again, we're really excited about. And that basically concludes my updates from a public safety standpoint. Is there any questions or anything anybody would like to discuss? I got a quick question about the drones. Is that something that could be leveraged for, say, like the balloon where you have the drone, you know, to be watching for potential, you know, crazy threats or something like that? Sure. Sure. No, absolutely. That's a great question. So, like, as I stated, we've had drone capabilities, so at large-scale events, they had drones up from a public safety standpoint. These drones, we have four drones, two of them are the DFR drones, so these are going to be specifically used to respond north or south to get those 90-second, you know, reconnaissance intel coming in to what's going on on the scene. In addition to that, we were forward-thinking and laying out this program, the two DFR drones are specifically just for that, to respond to the initial scene and, you know, the negative with any type of technology like this is battery life. So, when we deploy the drone, as the drone, you know, depending on weather conditions and how far it has to travel, that battery power gets chewed up pretty quickly, so it's a resource, just like everything else, and it's a great tool, but it's just that, a tool. So, for those prolonged incidents where we're going to need drone coverage or a proactive planned event, such as the balloon parade, is what you were asking, Paul, we have assigned one mobile drone to the police department and one mobile drone to the fire department. So, for instance, they had an incident last night, an emergency situation up in Springdale where it was a pretty high-profile crime, and even in this trial phase where everybody's kind of working through our training protocols, they had a drone up there for about an hour and a half ongoing. They would rotate them out, and it was pretty seamless. It was very impressive on my end to see how quickly this program has come together with the trainers and the people involved. It's very technical. There's a lot to think about, but, you know, again, just last night was, it's worth its weight in gold, in my opinion, to have that resource up there. But, yes, it will be available. We will have the drones available to work those large-scale events. That's something that, you know, is one of our biggest concerns. Large-scale events are very difficult to manage. We do a great job in planning and doing everything we can, and I think by adding this drone capability at large-scale events, it's just going to make us that more effective. Any other questions? All right, well, again, you have the sheet. We'll probably be doing, you know, when we come up with the date that we're actually going to launch, which, again, would be the first week of September at some point, we're going to be doing a press release. So, I encourage you all to look out for that, and then keep your ears and eyes open because hopefully we have some successful incidents with our drone coverage and our drone program in the upcoming weeks and months. So, with that said, that's item six, and the last thing on our agenda is to adjourn, so I'll take a motion to adjourn. Motion to adjourn. All right. Second? Second. All right. Meeting's adjourned. Thank you, everyone, for your time, and I look forward to talking to you guys soon. Thank you so much. All right. Thanks again, everybody.
